title: thoughts
content:
I would build the roadmap around this positioning:

> **OpenMaui is the Wayland-first, self-rendered, production-grade Linux platform for .NET MAUI — with X11 compatibility rather than GTK as its architectural foundation.**

Microsoft is still calling its GTK4 backend experimental and unsupported, despite now documenting and distributing it. That gives you a window to establish the production story before their backend matures. ([Microsoft Learn][1])

### 1. Make GPU-native Wayland presentation the highest technical priority

This is the biggest thing I would change.

Your current pipeline is essentially:

```text
MAUI
 ↓
SkiaView
 ↓
SKBitmap CPU raster
 ↓
pixel buffer
 ↓
wl_shm / XPutImage
 ↓
compositor
```

I would evolve it toward:

```text
MAUI
 ↓
SkiaView
 ↓
GPU-backed Skia surface
 ↓
EGL/OpenGL → Vulkan
 ↓
DMA-BUF / Wayland buffer
 ↓
compositor
```

with the current path retained as a fallback.

Architecturally, I'd probably introduce another boundary below `SkiaRenderingEngine`, something conceptually like:

```text
IRenderTarget
├── WaylandGpuRenderTarget
├── WaylandShmRenderTarget
├── X11GpuRenderTarget
└── X11RasterRenderTarget
```

Then `IDisplayWindow` remains responsible for display/input/window semantics rather than also determining how rendered pixels get there.

This matters because **right now GTK4 can legitimately argue that GSK/Vulkan gives it a sophisticated accelerated pipeline**. Once OpenMaui has direct GPU-backed Skia → Wayland presentation, your architectural argument becomes substantially stronger.

Then benchmark it.

Don't say:

> OpenMaui should be faster because there are fewer layers.

Say:

> Here are the numbers.

Measure startup, idle CPU, memory, scrolling FPS, frame time p95/p99, resize latency, animation smoothness, 1,000/10,000 item virtualization, text rendering and power consumption.

That transforms an architectural theory into evidence.

---

### 2. I would make WPE WebKit a major strategic project

This one is particularly interesting because something happened **four days ago** that fits OpenMaui almost perfectly.

WPE WebKit 2.54 was released September 16, 2026. Its new **WPEPlatform API is now stable**, and WPE is explicitly designed to embed WebKit **without requiring a UI toolkit like GTK**. It includes a native Wayland backend, supports GPU buffers through DMA-BUF with shared-memory fallback, and its web-process compositor now uses **Skia**. ([WPE][2])

That is almost tailor-made for OpenMaui.

Your current Wayland WebView is one of the architectural rough spots because WebKitGTK can't simply be reparented into a native Wayland window like it can under X11. Your own code consequently has special behavior around WebKitGTK/X11.

Imagine instead:

```text
OpenMaui
    │
    ├── Skia MAUI controls
    │
    └── WPE WebKit
           ↓
       WPEPlatform
           ↓
       GPU buffer / DMA-BUF
           ↓
         Wayland
```

WPE specifically exposes rendered web content through `WPEBuffer`, including DMA-BUF and SHM, without imposing GTK widgets on the embedding application. ([WPE][3])

And WPE 2.54 itself now uses Skia internally.

That gives you an unusually coherent stack.

I'd target:

```text
OpenMaui WebView
     ↓
WPE WebKit on native Wayland
WebKitGTK on X11 fallback
```

Then immediately build:

**BlazorWebView support.**

Microsoft's Linux GTK4 backend already lists WebKitGTK as its Blazor dependency. ([Microsoft Learn][4])

You do not want Microsoft to have:

> "MAUI Blazor works on Linux"

while OpenMaui says:

> "We're working on it."

Getting native Wayland `WebView` + `BlazorWebView` working through WPE would actually let you leapfrog them architecturally rather than merely reach parity.

---

### 3. Build a brutal compatibility/conformance suite

This may matter even more commercially than another 20 features.

Create something like:

```text
OpenMaui Compatibility Suite
```

Every release should automatically prove:

```text
MAUI Controls
████████████████████ 100%

MAUI Navigation
████████████████████ 100%

MAUI Essentials
███████████████████░  96%

MAUI Community Toolkit
██████████████████░░  91%

Blazor Hybrid
████████████████████ 100%

XAML
████████████████████ 100%
```

Not marketing percentages—actual tests behind every cell.

Run upstream MAUI sample applications wherever licensing allows. Test:

* XAML
* bindings
* styles
* triggers
* VisualStateManager
* animations
* Shell
* NavigationPage
* multi-window
* gestures
* accessibility
* clipboard
* DnD
* IME
* localization
* RTL/BiDi
* high DPI
* fractional DPI
* theme switching
* Toolkit controls

Most importantly, have **golden screenshot regression testing**.

If a 1.5× fractional-scale change makes an Entry move by two pixels, CI should catch it.

### 4. CI needs to become a competitive weapon

I don't see a public `.github/workflows` directory in the current repository. You have substantial tests, but the public project should visibly demonstrate that every commit is tortured across Linux configurations.

I would build a matrix resembling:

```text
                    GNOME     KDE      Weston/Sway
Ubuntu Wayland        ✓        ✓           ✓
Fedora Wayland        ✓        ✓           ✓
Ubuntu X11            ✓        —           —
Fedora X11            ✓        —           —
XWayland              ✓        ✓           ✓
```

Then hardware/build matrix:

```text
x64
ARM64

Intel Mesa
AMD Mesa
NVIDIA

1.0x
1.25x
1.5x
1.75x
2.0x
```

Obviously not every combination needs to run on every commit; divide it into PR, nightly and release qualification.

But publicly visible green matrices create confidence.

A developer considering:

```text
Microsoft experimental GTK backend

vs.

OpenMaui
```

should immediately see that OpenMaui is tested on real Linux environments much more aggressively.

---

### 5. Go all-in on Wayland, but don't abandon X11

Your existing architecture gives you exactly the right strategy.

I'd define:

```text
Wayland = primary architecture

X11/XWayland = compatibility architecture
```

Not:

```text
Wayland + X11 = equal future investment
```

Keep X11 rock-solid.

But new capabilities should normally be designed Wayland-first.

Examples:

* DMA-BUF
* presentation timing
* pointer constraints
* relative pointer
* tablet protocols
* activation
* idle inhibit
* color management
* HDR when appropriate
* screen capture via portals
* modern clipboard/DnD
* modern input methods

Then backport where practical.

That way OpenMaui is moving **with Linux**, rather than spending equal engineering effort on the architecture Linux is gradually leaving behind.

---

### 6. Make `xdg-desktop-portal` first-class

This is another strategic area I would prioritize highly.

Direct native integration is excellent, but modern sandboxed Linux applications increasingly interact with desktop capabilities through portals.

Create a proper OpenMaui portal layer for:

```text
FileChooser
OpenURI
Notifications
Screenshot
ScreenCast
Secret
Settings
Inhibit
Background
Print
RemoteDesktop
```

where appropriate.

Then your architecture becomes:

```text
                    OpenMaui
                       │
              ┌────────┴─────────┐
              ↓                  ↓
       Native Wayland       XDG Portals
              ↓                  ↓
       compositor APIs     desktop services
```

That is a very modern Linux platform architecture.

And it sets you up properly for Flatpak.

---

### 7. AppImage isn't enough: own Linux deployment

AppImage is a very good start.

I would add:

```text
dotnet openmaui publish appimage
dotnet openmaui publish flatpak
dotnet openmaui publish deb
dotnet openmaui publish rpm
```

Eventually perhaps Snap too.

And I'd create:

```bash
dotnet openmaui doctor
```

that prints something like:

```text
OpenMaui Environment

✓ .NET 10.0.4
✓ Wayland session
✓ Mutter 49
✓ fractional-scale-v1
✓ text-input-v3
✓ DMA-BUF
✓ WPE WebKit 2.54
✓ GStreamer
✓ CUPS
✓ AT-SPI2

GPU: AMD Radeon 7900 XTX
Renderer: Vulkan
Scale: 1.5x

OpenMaui: Ready
```

That tool alone would eliminate a huge amount of Linux support friction.

---

### 8. ARM64 should be first-class

Linux's future isn't exclusively x86.

Make sure OpenMaui is boringly reliable on:

```text
x86-64
ARM64
```

That opens:

* Raspberry Pi
* NVIDIA Jetson
* ARM development machines
* kiosks
* industrial devices
* thin clients
* edge AI systems

And here's where WPE becomes even more interesting: WPE is explicitly designed around embedded Linux and supports Wayland, DRM/KMS and headless operation. ([WPE][3])

OpenMaui + WPE + direct DRM/KMS could eventually create an entirely different market:

```text
.NET MAUI
   ↓
OpenMaui
   ↓
Skia/WPE
   ↓
DRM/KMS
```

No desktop environment required.

That's industrial/kiosk territory, not merely Linux desktop.

---

### 9. Make third-party MAUI compatibility a KPI

Once the fundamentals above are done, the metric I would chase isn't:

> We have 72 controls.

It would be:

> **How many existing MAUI applications compile and run without modification?**

I'd specifically test:

* CommunityToolkit.Maui
* CommunityToolkit.Maui.MediaElement
* SkiaSharp.Views.Maui
* LiveCharts2
* Maps
* popular MVVM frameworks
* dependency injection libraries
* logging libraries
* ReactiveUI
* graphics libraries

Then talk to Syncfusion, Telerik and DevExpress.

If one of them can say:

> "Our MAUI controls now run on Linux through OpenMaui"

that is worth far more strategically than another dozen built-in controls.

---

### 10. Establish a stable-contract/LTS story

Microsoft has an institutional advantage.

Your counterweight has to be predictability.

I would eventually define:

```text
OpenMaui 10 LTS
```

with a compatibility commitment:

> Apps targeting OpenMaui 10.x will continue to run across the supported .NET MAUI 10 lifecycle except where upstream breaking changes make that impossible.

Then use:

* semantic versioning
* API compatibility checks
* migration guides
* documented support matrix
* release candidates
* deterministic release cadence

Developers tolerate small open-source teams.

What scares enterprises is unpredictability.

---

### And I would change the messaging

Don't make the marketing battle:

> **OpenMaui vs GTK**

GTK is a very good toolkit. You'll eventually lose credibility with Linux developers if OpenMaui sounds hostile to it.

Instead:

> **OpenMaui uses the best Linux technologies where they make sense, without making any one desktop toolkit the foundation of MAUI.**

That's exactly what the code is already doing.

GTK/WebKit/etc. can be implementation tools.

But your architecture remains:

```text
MAUI
 ↓
OpenMaui
 ↓
Skia + Linux platform APIs
 ↓
Wayland
```

That is much more interesting.

## If I had 100 engineering points

I would allocate them roughly like this:

| Investment                                         | Points |
| -------------------------------------------------- | -----: |
| GPU-native Skia/Wayland rendering                  | **25** |
| WPE WebView + BlazorWebView                        | **20** |
| CI/conformance/visual regression/performance suite | **20** |
| XDG portals + Flatpak/deployment                   | **12** |
| MAUI/Toolkit compatibility                         | **10** |
| ARM64/embedded hardening                           |  **5** |
| Developer tooling / `openmaui doctor`              |  **5** |
| Additional controls/features                       |  **3** |

That last number is deliberate.

**You don't need another 30 controls right now.**

You need to make the existing 50+ controls run on a platform architecture that developers look at and think:

> "This is clearly engineered for where Linux is going."

And there's one particularly timely opportunity I would investigate immediately: **WPE WebKit 2.54.** It became stable essentially this week, uses Skia internally, is toolkit-independent, supports native Wayland, and exposes DMA-BUF-backed rendered buffers. ([WPE][2])

That sounds almost suspiciously well aligned with what you've already built.

If you execute **GPU-native Wayland + WPE/Blazor + exhaustive compatibility CI**, I think that creates a much deeper moat than simply staying ahead of Microsoft's GTK backend on feature count.

[1]: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/maui/developer-tools/platform-backends/?view=net-maui-10.0 ".NET MAUI experimental platform backends - .NET MAUI | Microsoft Learn"
[2]: https://wpewebkit.org/blog/2026-09-16-wpewebkit-2.54.html "WPE WebKit 2.54 highlights"
[3]: https://wpewebkit.org/about/architecture.html "WPE Architecture"
[4]: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/maui/developer-tools/platform-backends/linux-gtk4?view=net-maui-10.0 ".NET MAUI Linux GTK4 backend - .NET MAUI | Microsoft Learn"
